collection.title: Variable penetrance of schizophrenia in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with impaired, but reversible, neuronal mitophagy.
collection.authors: Stronati, E.; Rossano, A. J.; Li, J.; Stoesser, A. R.; Wallace, D. C.; Giulivi, C.; Anderson, S. A.
collection.abstract: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22qDS) is a major genetic risk factor for schizophrenia (Sz). We found that iPSC-derived neurons (iNeurons) from 22qDS +Sz individuals exhibit weaker mitochondrial energetics, whereas iNeurons from individuals with the same deletion but no psychosis (22qDS -Sz) upregulate expression of mitochondrial biogenesis-related genes. Here, we investigated why the +Sz group fails to undergo this compensation, finding that 22qDS +Sz iNeurons have older and more depolarized mitochondria than 22qDS -Sz or controls. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed downregulation of mitophagy-related pathways, and live imaging revealed elevated lysosomal pH. Restoring lysosomal acidity with acidifying nanoparticles improved mitophagy and, remarkably, increased the expression of mitochondrial biogenesis-related transcription factors in the +Sz neurons. We conclude that lysosomal dysfunction and impaired mitophagy differentiate 22qDS individuals who develop schizophrenia from those who do not. Mitophagy could be a novel therapeutic or preventative opportunity for Sz in the context of genetic neurodevelopmental disorders.

collection.title: A Unified Framework for Self-Recognition Across Monkeys, Infants, and Robots
collection.authors: Zhang, W.; Chen, K.; Zhang, T.; Sun, Q.; Sun, Y.; Jia, Y.; Chang, L.; Liu, J.; Qian, H.; Qin, P.; Jiang, F.; Wang, G.; Gong, N.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Institute of Neuroscience, Center for Excellence in Brain Science and Intelligence Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai, China.
collection.abstract: Self-recognition is a basic cognitive ability that indicates self-consciousness in humans. However, whether non-human agents such as monkeys and robots can possess a similar sense of self remains debated. Here, we develop a multi-scenario apparatus to examine self-recognition from different perspectives across macaque monkeys, human infants, and simulated robots. Monkeys trained for mirror-perspective (MP) self-face recognition were able to spontaneously recognize themselves when viewing video images of their back from a third-person perspective (3PP); however, this generalization required a few minutes of "exploration". In contrast, monkeys trained for 3PP self-back recognition spontaneously demonstrated MP self-recognition within seconds. Meanwhile, first-person-perspective (1PP) self-hand recognition represented a more basic ability that naive monkeys could achieve naturally. Interestingly, human infants aged 1 to 2 years exhibited a stepwise developmental sequence of 1PP, MP, and 3PP self-recognition abilities, consistent with the hierarchical levels of self-recognition in monkeys. Furthermore, we constructed world-model-based simulated robots and found that robots equipped with a body schema exhibited the emergence of self-recognition ability following multisensory integration training, along with the spontaneous generalization of self-recognition across different perspectives. Notably, the formation of internal self-body maps was identified as a key factor enabling this generalization. The convergence of findings across humans, monkeys, and robots not only redefines the evolutionary continuity of the self but also provides an operational framework for designing artificial systems capable of locating themselves in the world.

collection.title: Distal inhibition is recruited for action but not sensation in the primate superior colliculus
collection.authors: Bourrelly, C.; Yang, F.; Gandhi, N. J.
collection.abstract: Sensorimotor transformation requires neural circuits to coordinate excitation and inhibition, but how and whether this organization changes as the circuit transitions from processing sensation to action remain unresolved. We recorded laminar local field potentials across superior colliculus (SC) layers in four male macaques and computed current source density to resolve transmembrane currents during saccades to a target at one of eight isoradial directions. During the visual response, excitation was spatially confined to the receptive field, with little modulation at distant sites. During saccade generation, local excitation remained strongest for movements toward the receptive field, while inhibition extended across the SC map, including locations where spiking remained at baseline. Because the same recordings detected distal inhibition during movement, its absence during vision cannot reflect insufficient sensitivity, indicating that distal inhibition is selectively recruited during action. After saccade completion, excitation emerged regardless of saccade direction, potentially reflecting a rebound from, or release of, the preceding inhibition. These patterns were only partly reflected in spiking activity, which primarily captured local excitation, unmasking circuit dynamics largely invisible at the level of neuronal output. Together, our findings reveal a striking reconfiguration of SC population dynamics across sensorimotor transformation, spanning from spatially restricted excitation during sensation, to local excitation coupled with distal inhibition during movement generation, then to global post-movement excitation. Thus, fixed circuit architecture can express a sequence of behaviorally gated excitation-inhibition states largely invisible to spiking output.
